utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. Actually, if you have many questions in re-examination, we could take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, we can resume after the break. I don't have too many questions, but perhaps we can continue after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we take now a 15-minute break. But may I ask you whether you could kindly hand in the list of witnesses for next week with the precise indication of those Defence counsel who are calling those witnesses? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let me apologise to Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. Actually, your document had been filed, so we have now six witnesses for next week. Thank you. All right. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President Re-examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Divkovic, only a few questions. You said, regarding this decision on the appointment of a temporary board of managers, Defence Exhibit D52/2, that the SPS and Vitezit and Sintevit were actually socially-owned enterprises, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this decision relieving you of your duties, in fact, those enterprises are renamed, their ownership is being changed, in fact, and they're being called public corporations, public enterprises. Public enterprises are those managed by the state, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the structure of the enterprise, which was a socially-owned enterprise, could you be relieved of your duties by the government?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this was a socially-owned enterprise, the government did not have the authority to appoint or relieve general managers. It was the workers council who had that authority, the workers council of the enterprise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, this decision includes an untruth, an incorrect fact, calling Vitezit a public corporation whereby the government would have the right to take such decisions?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: They appropriated this right to rename the enterprise from a socially-owned one into a public one and thereby to be able to appoint and dismiss managers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we look at it from that standpoint, we can say that it was quite illegal as a document?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason that it was not implemented was not only that the new manager refused to implement it but also because the enterprise was incorrectly named because of procedural reasons?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: The measures taken beforehand illegally, anyway, could not have been implemented by me but only by the person they appointed, and at the end it says that instructions are given to the provisional manager to carry out this decision and to register the company with the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please will you look once again at document D55/2? In view of what Mr. Blaxill said, that there were no bills from 1993 or invoices addressed to the BH army, will you please look at page 1 where the numbers of the invoices are given?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And will you look whether there are any invoices from 1993 which have been included in this specification of claims?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course there are. All these numbers, stroke '92, '92, and then there's stroke '93, '93, '93, this is an indication that the goods were dispatched in 1993 and they were, in fact, dispatched then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the amounts vary between 369.000 German marks then to 46.000, 24.000, so these are large quantities of goods, obviously?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also tell us about the documents you brought with you? I didn't have them translated because I thought they would be too numerous. These are invoices and bills of lading for various goods. Are those the invoices on the basis of which these specifications were drafted and how did you gain possession of them?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: The papers that I handed to you include invoices on the basis of which goods were dispatched in the course of 1992. They were taken from the commercial department of the enterprise, and on the basis of those invoices and additional ones for 1993, these specifications were drawn up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, what is the main reason that the Lasva Valley or the part that remained under HVO control was not captured by the BH army during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Probably the main reason which contributed to the defence of this area was this factory and the vast amount of explosives in it, so that we could continue to produce those military ammunitions during the war, and that was the main factor that made it possible for the people there to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even though the superiority of the BH army was quite significant in manpower?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, five, six, or seven times superior in numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us where you spent the war, what you were doing.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I spent the war in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a soldier in the trench?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: For a time, I worked in the factory, in the finance department, and the rest of the time I was in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, there is no English translation. Kindly repeat what you said again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: From the questions put by the Prosecutor, I see that he doesn't quite understand the distinction between a socially-owned enterprise and a public enterprise in the former Yugoslavia, and I understand that because these are concepts from a socialist system that has failed, so let me try and explain so as to give you an idea of what this means. Re-examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So will you please describe for the benefit of the Court the difference between a social and a public enterprise?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I shall try and do so as far as my knowledge allows, though I am not an expert. A social enterprise means that it is owned by those people employed in it, by the workers in it, working in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who managed it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: They elected the management board, which was the workers council, and the members of the workers councils were elected at assembly meetings of workers, as they were called. The manager would be appointed by the board of management, in that case the workers council, and the manager is responsible to the workers council and reports to the workers counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a public enterprise?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: A public enterprise is one where the majority stockowner is the state, and then the state has the authority to appoint and dismiss managers, and managers report to the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, which body had a list of enterprises?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: The basic courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were no economic courts?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, the basic court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was called a register of economic organisations, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: You had to register the enterprise there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the register of enterprises, was it clearly indicated which enterprise was a public enterprise and which was a social one?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. The ownership of an enterprise has to be indicated and registered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any change from a social to a public enterprise, could it take place without first being registered before this change of ownership being registered in the register?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the rump government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, could it have, without changing this ownership in the register, change the ownership of an enterprise by its own decision?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: The government couldn't legally decide when it was a rump government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let us leave that aside.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, secondly, the government could not take such a decision without the procedure being carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So any change comes into effect only once it is entered in the register?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any specific characteristics in view of the fact that this was a special purpose industry, as it was called? Were there any special rules regarding management of such military institutions?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I have enough information to give you a clear answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So we'll limit ourselves to what we said. There were no changes in ownership that were registered in the economic register.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: No. All those enterprises were registered as social enterprises until the conflict, until the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have a question. May I direct your attention to Exhibit D55/2? I think probably it is in front of you. This one. Now, on page 1, I wonder whether you could clarify a couple of points? On the left, you have the ordinal number, and it struck me that the sequence is not very logical because you have, for instance, on the part concerning the shipments to Visoko, you have '92, then '93, '93, so four times '93, and then you go back to '92. Now, what is even more striking is that down below, again Visoko, if you look at the right, you have Visoko, Travnik, and then again Visoko. You have 9024/93, and then underneath 9172/92. Now, these are shipments to Visoko. What is the logic of this strange way of ordering in a chronological sequence? Is it because it was just a job done in a very sloppy way, or is there a logic behind this chronological sequence?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: I think there's no logic behind it, simply people didn't take care of the chronology of dates. After each of these invoices or, rather, there is the appropriate invoice to match each of the entries on this specification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This was a document -- because it's again not very clear what sort of document this is. This is a document prepared by the company, and when? By an accountant or -- there's no date, no signature.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DIVKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a specification of claims prepared after the war when we tried to collect our claims from the BH army and the HVO, and the document was compiled in the commercial sector on the basis of these invoices and dispatch papers. It is meant as evidence of our outstanding claims towards the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume there are no objections to the witness being released. Thank you so much for coming to The Hague to give evidence in court. You may now be released. I assume we can move on to our next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, who is going to be our next witness? Counsel Radovic? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you please read out the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like Prosecution Exhibit P1 to be shown to the witness and placed on the ELMO, because probably in the course of my examination of this witness I will need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Counsel Radovic, we don't know the name of this particular witness, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague has just reminded me of the proper procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, will you give us your name?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: My name is Rudo Kurevija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: 26th of August 1954.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you were born?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: I was born in Mali Mosunj, a settlement three kilometres west of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which municipality is that?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness has been introduced. He's not asking for any particular protective measures, so that his entire examination can be done in open session of the Trial Chamber. Could Prosecution Exhibit P1 be placed on the ELMO, because in the course of the examination of this witness we'll have to point to some places on that aerial photograph -- aerial map. Will you, witness, please look at this aerial photograph and show us your place of birth, Vitez and Ahmici so that Their Honours have an idea where you're from and how far that is from Vitez and Ahmici. The witness will be talking about military issues rather than political or economic issues.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: This is Mali Mosunj. It is this here, this part. The town of Vitez is here, and Ahmici is in the eastern part of Vitez municipality. So the place I was born is west of the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how far that is, as the crow flies, from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: I don't know exactly but about three and a half kilometres by road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from Ahmici how far is that?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: At least up to the crossroads and the turnoff for Ahmici. Vitez is about halfway there. Therefore, my birthplace is about six kilometres from Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you now tell us what qualifications you have and what you did until the free elections?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: I graduated from secondary engineering school in Novi Travnik. I worked until the end of 1991 in the maintenance facility in Travnik, which did repairs on military communications. So I was working as a civilian. In 1991 I was suspended, rather, my employment was terminated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: In August 1991 a protest rally was organised in Vitez. The intention and demand being that young men from Bosnia and Herzegovina should not be sent to serve in the former JNA outside the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who organised that rally?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: The HDZ of Vitez. Since I was on the video recording as one of the thousand participants at that rally, and since I was working in an institution that was doing maintenance of communications equipment for the JNA, that rally was interpreted as being directed against the JNA and, as such, my contract was terminated on the 23rd of December, 1991. I received a summons to court in Belgrade. Since I didn't dare go to Belgrade, because the conditions were such that I didn't have the courage to go there, after that I got a decision from the Military Tribunal dismissing me from employment. So I was unemployed, and the first job I got was in January 1995 when I worked in the Kalvarija enterprise as an accountant, and I'm still working there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this second employment was after the war? The job that you got in 1995 was after the war; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes. But as I said, I worked in this maintenance and repair facility in the JNA as an accountant in the purchasing department, procurement department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, what did you do when you found yourself unemployed in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: I was in Travnik at the time because my company was in Travnik. Since I had three children, of course my situation was an extremely difficult one. I didn't know how I would be able to survive, so I did farming and I had a miniature pig farm, and I made a living in that way and to provide a livelihood for my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you join in the activities of any party?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: I was a member of the party but not then, not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do as a member of the party? Did you have any position in the party?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: At the end of '91 -- or, rather, the beginning of 1992, I was elected as the President of the basic branch of HDZ for Mali Mosunj. It is one of the 21 basic branches of the HDZ, and I was president of that basic branch in Mali Mosunj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us how long you remained president of that branch? I'm not asking you for the exact date but roughly?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Until about the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which day do you consider to be the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: The 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As president of the basic board, did you have any influence or any possibility to influence the policy making of your party?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: As the president, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the policies were decided at another level?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: The municipal board was organised as follows: Within the municipal organisation there were municipal boards consisting of 17 members, and that was the highest body of the political organisation at the municipal level, and they were the ones who decided the policies and adopted documents, and they were the highest body. They were the creators of the policy of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you're talking about this highest body, you're referring to the HDZ part and its highest party. Tell me, was the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina organised according to the principle used in Communism known as Democratic Centralism? Were decisions made from the top down?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes. The highest body was the Presidency of the BH-HDZ, and that is where the global policies were defined. Then those decisions were passed down to the level of the municipal boards and they were the ones who implemented those decisions and those policies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you -- what did you do as president of the basic branch?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: As president of the basic branch I mainly dealt with the day-to-day problems of the people in the place where I lived, the needs of the community, and as the president, of course, I tried to increase the membership of the party. In those days new members joined. We collected membership fees and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, within your village and the place where you were the President of the basic branch of the political party of the HDZ, what was the ethnic composition of the population in Mali Mosunj?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: The place of my birth and where I live, the population is exclusively Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were no Muslim-Croat problems in your village because it was a single ethnic, one nation village. Do you know anything about the events in Vitez itself as the municipal seat after the free elections, how the municipal authorities were formed and whether this formation had any influence or any effect on your position as president of the basic branch?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything much about that. I worked in Travnik for 17 years, so all my connections were in Travnik. After I was dismissed from my job, I stayed at home, I stayed in my village, I was preoccupied with my problems, so I wasn't really active much in Vitez and I didn't take part as the President of the basic branch. I didn't participate in the formation of the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor in the development of relations between the HDZ and the SDA as if I understood you properly?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time did you, as a person who was struggling to make a livelihood by cultivating the land or -- how did you get information that the war against the Serbs had started?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: At the end of '91, so in the second half of '91 and the beginning of '92 we were listening to news reports about the war in Croatia. The people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I mean the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina took this tragically. There was a little bit of panic already amongst the people because we were aware, at least at that time I was aware, after the aggression against the Republic of Croatia, that aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina would follow. This was then confirmed by my conviction sometime in October '91, when the Yugoslav army attacked the village of Ravno near Trebinje. So it was then quite certain that Bosnia-Herzegovina was next, that parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be under attack by the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Ravno, this is in Herzegovina. What part of Herzegovina, eastern or western part?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Eastern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was this a village in Croatia? Was this a Croatian village?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes, Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can conclude this was one of the rare exclusively Croatian villages in eastern Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we could then say that this village was exclusively Croatian -- if you can pause between the answer and the question -- or did this village have some kind of important communications?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: It was mostly to round up or to encircle the territory that they were controlling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was the fate of the population of the village of Ravno?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were a lot of killed people. The village, as far as I know, was destroyed. The Croatian population was expelled from that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Croatians return to the village? Have they returned to date?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: I don't think that they have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After it became evident that the Serbs were capturing the territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina and war was being waged in Croatia at the same time, what did the people in your village do in order to protect themselves or for any other reason?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Well, as I said, the aggression against the Republic of Croatia that was taken deeply affected the people in my village, in the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was panic and fear among the Croatian population, and this was particularly evident after the events in the village of Ravno, near Trebinje. So that the people were afraid, crimes became more frequent, people began to organise themselves, at least that's what we did in Mosunj, in order to attempt to protect our village from criminals, and also out of the fear against -- out of the fear from the JNA and also this fear was exacerbated by the fact that in the Lasva Valley, there were members of the JNA in the barracks there which were located in the Lasva Valley, such as the barracks in Busovaca, then barracks in Travnik, an arms warehouse in Stojkovici, Novi Travnik, and in another location. So this was enough to be of concern to the people, so we tried to organise ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you try to organise yourselves? Did you do this alone, by yourselves?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes, we tried to self-organise. The bravest and the most loyal at that time, there were a lot of remnants from the old system at that time, so the most loyal ones we taught on how to protect the village, how to protect the people in the village, so that in my estimate, there were about ten or fifteen of us, and we were the village guard, we were patrolling at night, we were guarding the village, we were controlling the approaches and the exits to and from the village. So that we would carry out these watches at night, and then during the day, there was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us about the village guards. Until when did you participate in them, you personally?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: I personally participated in them until December of '92.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village guards, were they uniformed or was the village -- how was the village guard dressed? I am just asking this in this way in order not to suggest the answer.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Well, there were no uniforms. Everybody wore whatever they had at home, so it was civilian clothing, whatever we had at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: In the first few days, and then this went on for some time, we used hunting weapons. Mostly the hunters who had their weapons, they gave the weapons to the young men that they trusted so they could watch at night. There were people who had pistols, guns, and they had permits to carry those weapons. Mostly this is what we used in our patrols. If there were any shifts -- there was one shift until midnight, and then after midnight, there was another shift. We would give the weapons to the next shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, as far as I understood, that it was mostly weapons, mostly hunting weapons, that happened to be in the village. Did better weapons appear, for example, semiautomatic or automatic rifles, did they appear later, and if they did, how did they get to the village?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Of course, there were those who were better off in the village who had money at that time, and money didn't mean much at that time, so those that we trusted and who were better off, we talked with them and we collected money in this way. Many people sold their cattle, for example, in order to get money. So that's how we obtained weapons. We obtained the weapons exclusively on the black market because there were a lot of Serbs, in Travnik at least, and they generally had weapons in their houses, in their apartments, so since already in '92 they were already leaving Travnik, we would buy the weapons from them, so that's how we obtained our weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the men in your village, was there a certain number who had decided to fight outside the village?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think seven or eight men decided -- these were mostly young men who were unmarried, who didn't have so many obligations and duties and they were brave -- and then they decided to go and fight mostly in the region of Vlasic against the Serbs, they held the frontlines. Later they went to Jajce because there were a lot of problems up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of those seven young men, how many of them are still alive?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Unfortunately, three of them were killed. Two were killed already by mid '92, one of them was killed in August of '92. The first two were killed in taking the Slimena barracks, the barracks was also a weapons warehouse near Travnik, and these were the first casualties of the Serb aggression in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, were you personally present when Slimena was being captured?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe what this was like?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: There were about 50 of us volunteers from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the environs of Vitez, because you're not from Vitez itself?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: When I say Vitez, I mean the Vitez municipality, so there was about 50 of us. On the 3rd of May, we surrounded the Slimena barracks. There were some negotiations maybe for an hour or two, and since they were not willing to give up the barracks voluntarily without a fight, so there was fighting, it broke out in the afternoon, and the barracks were captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, during the capture of the barracks, were a part of the weapons damaged in the fighting or did the entire stock of weapons reach your hands?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Part of the warehouse was mined, it was blown up. Those people who were in the barracks managed to come out. A certain part of the weapons were destroyed. Since I was lightly wounded there myself, after the fighting was finished, I was transferred to Travnik, and I hear that people simply overran the barracks trying to obtain weapons in this way. So a part of the weapons ended up in the villages, the people had taken them, but then the next day, as I heard, the Muslims also tried to receive a share of the weapons that were confiscated in the barracks, and as far as I know, the outcome of that was an agreement to share the weapons 50-50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the action was carried out to capture Slimena, were only Croats in that action or did Muslims participate as well, or did the Muslims appear only later, after the barracks were captured?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Only Croats took part in this action, about 50 of us from Vitez. There was a number from Novi Travnik, but it was just Croats. The Muslims did not participate in this action, but they did appear on the next day, on the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the weapons were still distributed?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of weapons were there in Slimena; could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but there was infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: I mean weapons that infantry men use, like semiautomatic, automatic rifles. There was a certain amount of ammunition, mostly weapons from the Territorial Defence, because I think the TO from Central Bosnia was located in Slimena.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're talking about guns and ammunition regardless of whether these were automatic or semiautomatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Machine guns are also included among infantry weapons. Also mortars, they were also part of that, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible that there were some mortars, but I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then you did see the machine guns. Were there any cannons?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hand grenades?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether there were any mortars. I was wounded, so I was transferred, and whatever happened later, I wasn't in a position to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the development of the military component proceed among the Muslims and among the Croats, if you know, after the capture of Slimena, because a certain quantity of arms has appeared where a certain number of persons can be armed?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: After the capture of Slimena, more arms were available among the people in the villages, the people were better armed now, the village guards are growing in number, and I think at that time already the first units were being structured in Vitez and I think this was the active component, men who were active participants in that unit, and they were given the task to -- Vlasic and Jajce, to the frontlines there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, after the fall of Slimena or shortly before the fall of Slimena, were there any frontlines where Croats and Muslims fought together against the Serbs, and if there were, were they mixed units or were they separate units that were deployed next to one another?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Since I was not in the active force and I wasn't on the frontlines, I can't say anything about the Muslims. But as far as I know, Muslims were the ones -- Croats were the ones who were exclusively guarding on the frontlines, and this is from December in '92 until March of '93. For that period, I know that Croatian units, units of the HVO, were then holding the lines towards the Serbs near Novi Travnik, exclusively Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you, when we were talking about the village guards, these village guards, did they have a hierarchical structure? Were there any higher levels of command, or did it all remain within the village and its particular guard?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: There was no command structure for the village guards. They were just persons who had organised themselves. They made agreements among themselves. There were no commanders, no command staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but somebody had to keep a record or do some scheduling.

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: This was mostly done by agreement. Of course, at that time, because they were self-organised, these were young men who wanted to stay within the village, who wanted to guard their families, so there couldn't have been anybody who could have issued orders to them. Everybody had their own duties, obligations, so it wasn't possible to make a kind of plan of the watch, so we would just agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where the Croats from Central Bosnia fought against the Serbs? You mentioned Vlasic. Were there any other places?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: I don't know about Central Bosnia, but as far as we were concerned in Vitez, it was in Vlasic, Jajce. Then above Novi Travnik, there were positions, Kamenjar, Slatke Vode.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when Kotor Varos and Jajce fell, fell to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I don't know the exact date when Kotor Varos fell, but already, at the beginning of October in '92, the first expelled persons arrived in Vitez from the region of Kotor Varos and the surrounding villages, so that my village, Mali Mosunj, received 20 families. They were big families, they were expelled, so we gave them housing in our homes in the village. As far as Jajce is concerned, I think it fell later, but I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Serbs captured a certain territory, what was the fate of the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Of course, people were expelled, I assume their houses were burnt down, so I doubt that anybody remained in those regions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This applies both to Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the expelled people arrived from these areas that you mentioned, you mentioned people who were expelled who came to your village, and since this was a Croatian village, I assume that these were Croatian people who arrived?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes, they were exclusively Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what were the consequences of the conquest by the Serbs as far as Vitez is concerned? Did any displaced Muslims come to the Vitez region?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Muslim refugees came. Since my village borders on the Travnik-Vitez transit road where there are Muslim settlements, so the Muslim settlements of Bazen and Grbavica housed the Muslims who were expelled. They were situated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any differences in the treatment of these people after they were expelled? Did the Croats mostly stay in the region of Vitez or did they move further along, or did the Muslims remain in the region of Vitez or did they move along?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Of course, these 20 families that came to Mosunj and then the supplies to the other places where Croats were housed, they remained there very shortly. They considered Vitez as just a stopover. They remained maybe from the beginning of October to about maybe the 13th of October. They went through Vitez trying to reach Herzegovina or Croatia or Western countries because a lot of their families or relatives worked abroad, so that's where they would go. So they only stayed there for a very brief period of time, maybe for ten days. As far as Muslims are concerned, they stayed for quite a while. They remained there, and you could tell this. The villages are very small, we all know one another, and you could tell that Muslims remained because there were a lot of new faces, lots of unfamiliar people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when the refugees came to your area, did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: Rudo Kurevija
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There were a lot of soldiers who had fought in their villages. They carried their weapons with them. Since they were leaving Vitez they did not carry their weapons with them. Some of them would leave the weapons to the friends, the hosts who had put them up, but a lot of them sold these weapons in order -- so this is how certain quantities of weapons were obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm finished with this part of my examination, so if you agree, we could resume on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Monday then at 2.00, from 2.00 to 6.00.
